lessons.title: The Genome and Genetic Information
lessons.description: DNA, genes, alleles and how the genome shapes you, explored through real-world examples.
lessons.content_html:
What Is the Genome?

Imagine sending a cheek swab to a consumer DNA-testing company. Weeks later you receive a report listing your ancestry, a handful of health-related genetic variants, and perhaps a curiosity about whether you carry the gene for earwax type. All of that information comes from a single source: your genome. The genome is the complete collection of DNA found in virtually every cell of your body. Understanding how the genome is organised, how it stores information and how it shapes your characteristics is the starting point for all of genetics.

Inside the nucleus of most cells, DNA is packaged into thread-like structures called chromosomes. Humans have 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs. One chromosome of each pair came from your mother; the other came from your father. Each chromosome carries hundreds to thousands of shorter sections of DNA called genes. A single human genome contains tens of thousands of protein-coding genes, plus large regions of DNA that regulate gene activity.

Key Fact

The genome is the complete DNA of an organism. In humans, DNA is packaged into 46 chromosomes (23 pairs) inside the cell nucleus. Genes are short sections of DNA on chromosomes that code for specific proteins.

DNA — A Polymer of Nucleotides

DNA is a polymer — a long molecule assembled from many smaller repeating units. The repeating unit of DNA is the nucleotide, which consists of a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group, and one of four organic bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), or guanine (G). Two strands of nucleotides twist around each other to form the famous double helix shape.

The two strands are held together by the bases, which pair in a fixed, complementary way: A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G. This complementary base pairing is one of the most important rules in genetics. It means the sequence of bases on one strand automatically determines the sequence on the other, and it makes accurate copying of DNA possible before cell division.

The sequence of bases along the DNA acts as a code — a biological instruction manual. Every group of three consecutive bases (a triplet) codes for one specific amino acid. The order of these triplets along a gene determines which amino acids are assembled, in what order, at the ribosomes. Different sequences of amino acids fold into different protein shapes, and the shape of a protein determines its function. So ultimately, the base sequence in your DNA determines every protein your body makes.

Making a protein from a gene happens in two main stages. First, inside the nucleus, the relevant gene is used as a template to produce a molecule of mRNA (messenger RNA) — a single-stranded copy of the gene’s base sequence. This process is called transcription. The mRNA then travels out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm.

Second, the mRNA is read at a ribosome in a process called translation. The ribosome reads the base sequence three bases at a time, and for each triplet it recruits the matching amino acid. The amino acids are joined together in sequence to form a growing protein chain. Once complete, the chain folds into a specific three-dimensional shape — the shape that gives the protein its function.

Proteins carry out an enormous range of tasks. Enzymes catalyse chemical reactions. Structural proteins such as collagen give tissues strength. Hormones such as insulin regulate body processes. Antibodies defend against infection. All of these functions trace back to the DNA base sequence that coded for them.

Alleles: Different Versions of the Same Gene

Because you inherit one chromosome from each parent, you carry two copies of most genes — one on each chromosome of a pair. Different versions of the same gene are called alleles. For many genes, only one or two common alleles exist; for others, dozens of variants are known.

The particular combination of alleles a person carries is their genotype. The visible or measurable characteristic that results from those alleles interacting with the environment is the phenotype. Eye colour, blood group and whether your earlobes are attached or free are all examples of phenotypic characteristics with a genetic basis.

Key Fact

Alleles are different versions of the same gene. The genotype is the combination of alleles an organism has. The phenotype is the observable characteristic that results from the genotype and the environment.

How the Genome Shapes Your Characteristics

Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene, such as whether pea plants produce round or wrinkled seeds (the classic example studied by Gregor Mendel in his monastery garden experiments during the 1850s and 1860s). In humans, cystic fibrosis and certain blood groups are examples of single-gene traits. However, the vast majority of human characteristics — height, skin colour, intelligence, susceptibility to many diseases — are polygenic: influenced by many genes acting together.

On top of the genetic influence, the environment also shapes phenotype. A person may carry genes associated with above-average height, but if they suffer from severe malnutrition in childhood their growth will be stunted. This interaction between genotype and environment explains why identical twins, who share the same DNA, are not exactly identical in every measurable trait.

An international scientific collaboration known as the Human Genome Project set out to read the entire sequence of base pairs in the human genome. The project published a working draft in the early 2000s. The completed sequence revealed that the human genome is around 3 billion base pairs long and contains tens of thousands of protein-coding genes, far fewer than many scientists had predicted.

The practical consequences have been far-reaching. Scientists can now identify specific gene variants linked to inherited conditions such as Huntington’s disease or breast cancer risk, enabling genetic testing and counselling. Researchers use genomic data to understand why some people respond differently to the same drug, opening the door to personalised medicine tailored to a patient’s genetic profile.

Consumer DNA tests — the kind that arrive from a cheek swab — use a fraction of this genomic knowledge to estimate ancestry and flag certain variants. They are a striking example of how fundamental genetic science has moved from laboratory curiosity to everyday life within a generation.

At higher tier, you may be asked about non-coding DNA. Not all of the genome codes for proteins. Large sections regulate when and where genes are switched on or off. Mutations in regulatory regions can affect gene expression without altering the protein sequence itself, which can have significant effects on development and disease risk.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions about genetics often use command words like ‘explain’ or ‘suggest’. When asked to explain how a base sequence determines a protein, use the word ‘because’: “The base sequence determines the order of amino acids because each triplet of bases codes for one amino acid.” Avoid just listing facts — link each point to its consequence. For extended-response questions involving the genome and society (genetic testing, personalised medicine), remember to evaluate both the scientific benefit and any social or ethical dimension.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The genome is the complete DNA of an organism, packaged into chromosomes in the cell nucleus. Genes are sections of DNA that code for proteins via a triplet base code.
  • Alleles are different versions of the same gene. The genotype (allele combination) interacts with the environment to produce the phenotype (observable characteristic).
  • Most human characteristics are polygenic, controlled by multiple genes and shaped by environment. Genomic science enables genetic testing and personalised medicine.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'genome'.

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure of DNA, including the role of base pairing.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: DNA is a double helix polymer made of two nucleotide strands. The strands are held together by complementary base pairs (A-T and C-G). [2 marks — 1 for double helix/polymer structure, 1 for complementary base pairing rule.]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a change in a gene's base sequence could affect the protein it codes for.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A change in the base sequence alters the triplet code; a different triplet codes for a different amino acid, so the amino acid sequence changes; this alters the folded shape of the protein, changing or destroying its function.
Secure: Altered base sequence → different amino acid sequence → different protein shape.
Developing: Altered sequence → different protein made.
Emerging: Change in DNA → change in protein.

practice_questions.text: Compare the genotype and phenotype of two individuals who both have brown eyes but different allele combinations for eye colour.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Individual A may be homozygous for the brown allele (BB); individual B may be heterozygous (Bb). Both have the same phenotype (brown eyes) because brown is dominant over blue, so the presence of even one B allele produces the brown phenotype. Their genotypes differ despite the same phenotype.
Secure: Different genotypes (BB and Bb) → same phenotype because brown allele is dominant.
Developing: One has two brown alleles; the other has one of each; both look the same.
Emerging: They have different alleles but the same eye colour.

practice_questions.text: A person receives their consumer genome report and discovers they carry a variant associated with increased risk of a particular condition. Explain why this does not mean they will definitely develop the condition, and describe one way this information could be used beneficially.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Many conditions are polygenic — multiple genes contribute — so one variant alone rarely determines outcome. Environmental factors (diet, exercise, exposure) also interact with genotype to shape phenotype. Beneficial use: the person could adopt lifestyle changes to reduce their environmental risk, or attend regular screening so any early signs are caught and treated promptly.
Secure: One variant doesn't guarantee illness because environment and other genes also matter; benefit — early screening or lifestyle changes.
Developing: Other things also cause the condition; they could go to the doctor more often.
Emerging: It's just a risk, not certain.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the benefits and limitations of using the human genome sequence to develop personalised medicine for inherited conditions.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates both sides with science. Benefits — identifying specific gene variants linked to conditions enables targeted drug selection and dosing; reduces trial-and-error prescribing; enables predictive genetic testing so at-risk individuals can take preventive action. Limitations — many conditions are polygenic and environmentally influenced, so genomic data alone cannot predict outcomes reliably; sequencing costs and data interpretation require specialist infrastructure; raises ethical questions about genetic privacy and insurance discrimination. Reaches a balanced conclusion weighing evidence.
Secure: Clear benefits (targeted treatment, early detection) and limitations (complexity, cost, ethics) with some development of each.
Developing: Lists a few benefits and limitations without linking to the science.
Emerging: One benefit and one limitation stated only.

lessons.title: Inheritance and Genetic Variants
lessons.description: Dominant and recessive alleles, Punnett squares, sex determination and inherited disease.
lessons.content_html:
A Family Pedigree — Why Do Traits Skip Generations?

Consider a family in which neither parent has cystic fibrosis, yet one of their children is diagnosed with the condition. The parents are shocked — neither of them shows any symptoms. How is this possible? The answer lies in the way alleles are inherited and in the distinction between dominant and recessive patterns of inheritance.

Dominant and Recessive Alleles

Not all alleles behave the same way. A dominant allele is always expressed in the phenotype, regardless of whether the person carries one copy or two. A recessive allele is only expressed when both copies of the gene are recessive — when no dominant allele is present to mask it.

An individual with two identical alleles for a gene is homozygous for that gene. An individual with two different alleles is heterozygous. Heterozygous individuals carrying one dominant and one recessive allele express the dominant phenotype but can pass the recessive allele to their offspring — they are carriers.

Key Fact

Dominant alleles are expressed when one or two copies are present. Recessive alleles are only expressed when both copies are recessive (homozygous recessive). Heterozygous carriers have one copy of a recessive allele but show the dominant phenotype.

Genotype, Phenotype and the Environment

The genotype describes the actual alleles an individual carries; the phenotype is the observable characteristic that results. An important point is that the phenotype can be influenced by the environment as well as by the genotype. For example, a plant may carry the genetic potential for maximum height, but if it is grown in poor soil it will not reach that height. In humans, identical twins share the same genotype but can differ in phenotype if they have lived in different environments, follow different diets or develop different health conditions. Single-gene traits such as cystic fibrosis or blood type are largely unaffected by the environment, whereas polygenic traits like height or intelligence are influenced significantly by both genes and environment combined.

Punnett Squares

A Punnett square is a systematic way to work out the probabilities of offspring genotypes. One parent’s alleles are written along the top of the grid; the other parent’s along the side. Each box in the grid shows one possible combination of alleles in an offspring — one allele from each parent.

Let F represent the dominant allele (no cystic fibrosis) and f represent the recessive allele (cystic fibrosis). Both parents in our family pedigree are carriers: their genotype is Ff. Here is the cross:

Parent 1 (Ff) × Parent 2 (Ff)

Gametes from Parent 1: F or f. Gametes from Parent 2: F or f.

Offspring possibilities: FF, Ff, Ff, ff — giving a 1 : 2 : 1 genotype ratio. The phenotype ratio is 3 unaffected : 1 with cystic fibrosis. Each child has a 25% (1 in 4) chance of having cystic fibrosis, a 50% chance of being a carrier, and a 25% chance of being homozygous dominant (not a carrier).

This explains the family scenario: the parents are both carriers (Ff) with no symptoms, but they each passed the recessive f allele to that child. The probabilities are independent for each pregnancy — having one affected child does not change the 25% probability for the next.

Key Fact

Crossing two carriers (Ff × Ff) gives offspring ratios of 1 FF : 2 Ff : 1 ff. The probability of the recessive phenotype is 25% per child. These are probabilities — actual outcomes vary with chance.

Cystic Fibrosis — A Recessive Inherited Condition

Cystic fibrosis is one of the most common serious inherited conditions in the UK. It is caused by a recessive allele, so a person needs two copies of the faulty allele (ff) to be affected. The faulty allele leads to the production of a defective version of a membrane protein that controls the movement of salt and water across cell surfaces. As a result, the mucus in the lungs and digestive tract becomes abnormally thick and sticky, obstructing airways and impairing digestion. Physiotherapy, enzyme supplements and respiratory treatments can manage symptoms, but the condition cannot currently be cured.

One pair of human chromosomes, the sex chromosomes, determines biological sex. Females carry two X chromosomes (XX); males carry one X and one Y chromosome (XY). During meiosis, gametes receive one sex chromosome each. All eggs carry an X chromosome. Sperm can carry either an X or a Y chromosome, each with equal probability.

At fertilisation: if a Y-bearing sperm fuses with the egg, the offspring is XY (male); if an X-bearing sperm fuses with the egg, the offspring is XX (female). A Punnett square for sex determination shows a 1 XX : 1 XY ratio — so there is a 50% probability that any given pregnancy will produce a male or female. The father’s sperm, not the mother’s egg, determines biological sex.

Polydactyly — A Dominant Inherited Condition

Polydactyly (extra fingers or toes) is caused by a dominant allele. A person needs only one copy of the dominant allele (D) to show the condition. Crossing an affected heterozygous parent (Dd) with an unaffected parent (dd) gives offspring genotypes of Dd and dd in a 1 : 1 ratio — a 50% chance per child. Because the allele is dominant, polydactyly can appear in every generation of a family, unlike recessive conditions which can skip generations when carried by heterozygous individuals.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In genetic cross questions, always show your working in full: write the parental phenotypes, write the parental genotypes, list the gametes, complete the Punnett square, then state the offspring genotype and phenotype ratios. Missing any of these steps can cost marks even if your final answer is correct. When the question says ‘suggest’, apply the science to the context given — you won’t recognise the scenario from revision, but you will have the rules to work it out.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Dominant alleles are expressed with one or two copies present; recessive alleles only show when both copies are recessive. Carriers are heterozygous individuals who carry a recessive allele without being affected.
  • Punnett squares predict offspring probabilities. Two carrier parents (Ff × Ff) give a 25% probability of an affected child per pregnancy — these are independent probabilities each time.
  • Cystic fibrosis is a recessive inherited condition. Sex is determined by the 23rd chromosome pair (XX female, XY male); the sperm determines the sex of the offspring.

practice_questions.marks: An individual who carries one copy of the recessive allele but does not show the condition (heterozygous). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what a Punnett square is used for and how it is constructed.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: A Punnett square predicts the possible genotypes (and phenotypes) of offspring. One parent's alleles are placed along the top; the other parent's alleles along the side; each box shows one possible offspring genotype. [2 marks — 1 for purpose, 1 for method of construction.]

practice_questions.text: A woman is a carrier for cystic fibrosis (Ff). Her partner does not carry the allele (FF). Explain the probability that their child will have cystic fibrosis.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Cross Ff × FF. Gametes: F or f (mother); F (father). Offspring genotypes: FF and Ff in a 1:1 ratio. No offspring can be ff, so the probability of cystic fibrosis is 0%. The father has no f allele to pass on, so the recessive phenotype cannot appear.
Secure: Punnett square shown; correct offspring genotypes; probability stated as 0% with reason.
Developing: States the child cannot have cystic fibrosis, but reasoning is incomplete.
Emerging: States one parent is a carrier but does not complete the cross.

practice_questions.text: Both parents are carriers of cystic fibrosis (Ff). They have four children. Suggest why it is possible that none of their children have cystic fibrosis, even though the predicted ratio is 3 unaffected : 1 affected.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The Punnett square gives probabilities (25% per child) based on the laws of chance. With only four children, it is entirely possible — though unlikely — for no child to inherit the ff genotype. Each pregnancy is an independent event; previous outcomes have no effect on the next. With small sample sizes, actual results often deviate significantly from predicted ratios.
Secure: Probabilities are independent per child; small sample sizes cause deviation from predicted ratios.
Developing: Probability doesn't guarantee the outcome; random chance.
Emerging: They might just be lucky.

practice_questions.text: Compare the pattern of inheritance of cystic fibrosis (recessive) with polydactyly (dominant) in a family pedigree.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Cystic fibrosis can skip generations because carriers (Ff) appear unaffected; two unaffected carrier parents can have an affected child. Polydactyly appears in every generation because only one copy of the dominant allele is needed; an affected individual has a 50% chance of passing it to each child if heterozygous. In a pedigree, recessive conditions appear sporadically; dominant conditions appear in every generation.
Secure: Cystic fibrosis skips generations; polydactyly appears in every generation; explanation linked to dominant/recessive allele behaviour.
Developing: One condition can skip generations; the other can't; some reason given.
Emerging: One is dominant, one is recessive.

practice_questions.text: A couple want to know whether future children could be affected by a genetic condition that runs in one partner's family. Evaluate the usefulness of genetic testing and Punnett square analysis in advising this couple.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Genetic testing can identify whether each partner carries a relevant allele, providing actual genotype data rather than family history estimates. Punnett square analysis can then calculate precise probabilities for each pregnancy outcome. Limitations: probability does not guarantee outcome; genetic testing is not always available for all conditions; results may cause anxiety or affect insurance/employment; some conditions are polygenic and cannot be predicted from a single gene test. A balanced conclusion notes that combined testing and counselling gives the most informed picture, while recognising uncertainty remains.
Secure: Benefits of testing (confirms genotype, allows probability calculation) and limitations (probabilistic only, ethical/emotional impact) addressed clearly.
Developing: Some benefits listed; one limitation mentioned.
Emerging: Testing is useful but might be worrying.

lessons.title: Gene Technology and Ethics
lessons.description: Genetic testing, embryo screening, gene therapy and how society weighs benefits against risks.
lessons.content_html:
When Science Meets Society

In 2001, a couple discovered through genetic testing that they had both inherited the allele for Huntington’s disease — a dominant, inherited condition that causes progressive brain damage, typically appearing in mid-life. They wanted children but feared passing the condition on. With the help of a specialist fertility clinic, embryos created outside the body were tested before implantation. Only embryos free of the allele were selected. Their daughter was born healthy and has no risk of inheriting Huntington’s from this allele.

This case illustrates the power and the complexity of modern gene technology. The science is real, the benefits can be life-changing — and the ethical questions it raises are genuinely difficult. This lesson walks through the key applications and the framework scientists and society use to weigh them.

Genetic Testing

Genetic testing can be carried out at different stages of life and for different purposes. Carrier testing identifies adults who carry a recessive allele for a condition such as cystic fibrosis or sickle cell anaemia, even though they are unaffected themselves. It helps couples understand their risk before having children. Predictive testing identifies whether someone carries an allele that will (or is likely to) cause a condition later in life, such as Huntington’s disease. Diagnostic testing confirms or rules out a suspected inherited condition after symptoms appear.

Genetic testing during pregnancy can be done by sampling foetal cells from the amniotic fluid (amniocentesis) or from the placenta (chorionic villus sampling). These tests carry a small risk to the pregnancy and are offered when there is an identified reason to suspect an inherited condition.

Key Fact

Genetic testing includes carrier testing (identifies carriers of recessive alleles), predictive testing (identifies future disease risk) and diagnostic testing (confirms a suspected condition). Each has genuine benefits and genuine risks that must be weighed carefully.

Embryo Screening — Pre-implantation Genetic Diagnosis

Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) allows couples who are carriers of serious genetic conditions to have children free of those conditions. Embryos are created outside the body using in vitro fertilisation (IVF). A cell is removed from each embryo at an early stage and its DNA is tested. Embryos that carry the faulty alleles are not implanted; those free of the condition are selected for implantation.

PGD is currently used in the UK for serious conditions including cystic fibrosis, Huntington’s disease, and certain chromosomal conditions. It is regulated by law — only conditions meeting defined criteria of seriousness can be screened for.

Benefits: Prevents the birth of children with serious, life-limiting conditions. Reduces suffering for affected individuals and their families. Enables people who carry genetic conditions to have biological children they might otherwise choose not to have. Reduces long-term healthcare costs associated with managing serious inherited conditions.

Risks and concerns: IVF itself carries medical risks for the woman (hormonal stimulation, procedure risks). Unused embryos are destroyed — people who believe life begins at fertilisation see this as morally problematic. There is a risk of ‘designer baby’ concerns: if embryo selection is permitted for medical conditions, could it slide towards selecting non-medical traits such as intelligence or appearance? This ‘slippery slope’ argument is taken seriously by many bioethicists. Some disability advocates argue that selecting against certain conditions implies that lives lived with those conditions are less valuable.

When weighing these considerations, scientists, regulators and individuals use a process of risk-benefit analysis under uncertainty. The decision is not purely scientific — it involves values, personal beliefs and social priorities alongside the evidence. This is why regulatory bodies include ethicists, patient representatives and lay members alongside scientists.

Gene Therapy

Gene therapy aims to treat or cure genetic conditions by delivering a working copy of the faulty gene into the patient’s cells. If the cells can then produce the normal protein, the symptoms of the condition are reduced or eliminated. Two main approaches exist:

Somatic gene therapy targets the body (somatic) cells of the patient. Any changes affect only that individual and are not passed on to children. This is the approach currently used in clinical trials and approved treatments. Germline gene therapy would target eggs, sperm or early embryos, meaning any changes would be inherited by future generations. Germline editing in humans is not permitted in the UK and most countries because the safety and ethical implications are not yet understood.

Key Fact

Somatic gene therapy targets body cells and affects only the patient. Germline gene therapy would affect all future generations and is not currently permitted in the UK due to unresolved safety and ethical concerns.

GM Crops and Agricultural Gene Technology

Genetically modified (GM) crops have had genes from other organisms introduced into their genome. A well-known example is Golden Rice, which has been engineered to produce beta-carotene (a precursor of vitamin A) in the grain, because rice does not naturally do this. Vitamin A deficiency is a serious public health problem in parts of the world where rice is the dietary staple. GM crops in general are also engineered for resistance to specific herbicides or insect pests, which can reduce pesticide use and increase yields.

Arguments in favour of GM crops: Could address vitamin deficiency and malnutrition in developing countries. Herbicide-resistant crops reduce the number of spraying applications needed. Higher yields can reduce pressure to clear new land for agriculture, potentially benefiting biodiversity. Peer-reviewed scientific consensus generally considers currently approved GM crops to be safe for consumption.

Arguments against GM crops: Modified genes could spread to wild plant relatives through cross-pollination, potentially creating herbicide-resistant weeds (‘superweeds’). Effects on non-target organisms (insects, birds) in the ecosystem are not always fully understood before release. Large seed companies that own GM seed patents could gain disproportionate economic power over farmers. Public trust is difficult to rebuild if problems emerge after widespread adoption. Some religious and cultural viewpoints object to ‘playing God’ by altering life at the genetic level.

Evaluating the GM debate well means distinguishing between claims that are supported by scientific evidence (e.g. peer-reviewed safety studies on specific approved crops) and claims that are ethical or value-based (e.g. concerns about corporate power or religious views). Both types of concern are legitimate inputs to a policy decision — but they carry different kinds of weight.

Making Ethical Decisions in Science

When scientists, governments and the public decide whether to permit a technology like PGD, gene therapy or GM crops, they rarely reach a consensus based on evidence alone. Ethical decision-making in science involves weighing the scientific evidence (does it work? what are the risks?) alongside values (what kind of society do we want? whose interests count?) and practicalities (who will have access? who bears the costs?).

In your exam, questions about gene technology and ethics will often ask you to ‘evaluate’ or ‘discuss’. This means presenting both the case for and the case against a technology, using scientific reasoning, and reaching a reasoned conclusion. Simply listing benefits without acknowledging risks, or dismissing a technology without engaging with its evidence base, will not reach the top marks.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Extended-response questions on gene technology are typically set in a context you won’t have seen before — for example, a news article about a new genetic test or a fictional family facing a decision about embryo screening. Use the context, apply the science, and evaluate both sides. Markers reward reasoning: why does this benefit matter? why does this risk concern people? A conclusion that says “the technology should be allowed, provided it is regulated” with reasons is stronger than “there are pros and cons.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Genetic testing (carrier, predictive, diagnostic) and PGD allow individuals to make informed reproductive decisions, but carry medical, ethical and social risks including concerns about embryo destruction and ‘designer baby’ fears.
  • Gene therapy aims to treat genetic conditions by delivering functional genes to patient cells. Somatic therapy is permitted; germline editing is not, due to unresolved safety and ethical issues.
  • GM crops offer potential benefits (nutrition, yield) but raise concerns about ecological impact and economic power. Sound ethical decisions require both scientific evidence and recognition of values — they are rarely purely scientific.

lessons.title: Causes of Disease and Pathogens
lessons.description: Communicable and non-communicable disease, how pathogens spread, and the body's first-line defences.
lessons.content_html:
An Outbreak in Context

In the winter of 2018–19, measles cases rose sharply across several European countries. Public health teams traced the outbreaks to communities with lower vaccination rates. The pathogen — the measles virus — spread rapidly through airborne droplets in schools and public spaces. At the same time, in the same communities, adults were being diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at record rates — a condition caused not by a pathogen but by a combination of lifestyle factors and genetic risk. These two parallel health crises illustrate the fundamental distinction at the heart of this lesson: communicable diseases versus non-communicable diseases.

What Is a Pathogen?

A pathogen is any microorganism capable of causing disease. There are four main types of pathogen, each with a distinct structure and way of causing harm:

Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes — they have no true nucleus. They reproduce rapidly by binary fission inside the host and cause illness mainly by releasing toxins that damage cells and tissues. Examples of bacterial diseases include tuberculosis (TB), salmonella food poisoning, and cholera.

Viruses are far smaller than bacteria and are not cells. They consist of genetic material — either DNA or RNA — surrounded by a protein coat. Viruses cannot replicate independently. They invade host cells, hijack the cell’s machinery to make copies of themselves, and then burst out of the cell, destroying it. This is what causes the symptoms of diseases such as influenza, measles, HIV, and COVID-19.

Fungi are eukaryotic organisms (with nuclei) that can cause disease in humans. Many fungal infections are superficial, affecting the skin, nails or hair (for example, athlete’s foot is caused by Tinea fungi). In individuals with weakened immune systems, fungi can cause more serious internal infections.

Protists are single-celled eukaryotes. The most medically significant protist is Plasmodium, which causes malaria. Plasmodium is transmitted via the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes, which act as a biological vector. The parasite multiplies inside red blood cells and the liver, causing cycles of fever, chills and anaemia.

Key Fact

The four types of pathogen are bacteria (reproduce and release toxins), viruses (invade cells and replicate inside them), fungi (cause surface or systemic infections) and protists (e.g. Plasmodium causing malaria via mosquito vectors).

How Communicable Diseases Spread

Understanding transmission routes is essential for controlling outbreaks. The main routes by which pathogens pass between hosts are:

Direct contact — the pathogen passes directly from one person to another through touch, or through sexual contact (e.g. HIV, chlamydia). Airborne droplets — when an infected person coughs, sneezes or speaks, tiny droplets containing pathogens are released into the air and can be inhaled by others nearby. Measles and influenza spread this way. Contaminated food or water — pathogens enter the digestive system when a person eats or drinks contaminated material. Salmonella and cholera are transmitted via this route. Animal vectors — organisms such as mosquitoes, ticks and fleas transmit pathogens when they bite or feed on hosts. Malaria is transmitted by mosquito vectors.

Salmonella is a bacterial disease transmitted through contaminated food, particularly raw or undercooked poultry and eggs. The bacteria produce toxins that cause vomiting, diarrhoea and fever. Proper cooking kills the bacteria; hygiene in food preparation prevents cross-contamination.

HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) is transmitted through bodily fluids, particularly blood, semen and breast milk. It attacks helper T lymphocytes, progressively damaging the immune system. Without treatment, HIV infection can progress to AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome), leaving the person unable to fight off infections that a healthy immune system would control easily. Antiretroviral drugs suppress HIV replication, allowing people to live healthy lives.

Cholera is a bacterial disease caused by Vibrio cholerae, transmitted through water or food contaminated with infected faeces. The bacteria produce a toxin that causes the intestinal wall to secrete massive amounts of water, leading to severe diarrhoea and dehydration. Cholera outbreaks typically follow disasters that disrupt clean water supplies. Oral rehydration therapy saves lives by replacing fluids and electrolytes.

The Body’s First Line of Defence: Barriers

The body does not wait passively for pathogens to enter — it maintains a series of physical and chemical barriers that prevent most pathogens from getting in at all. These non-specific defences act against all types of pathogen regardless of what they are:

Skin is the body’s largest organ and its primary physical barrier. It is made of tightly packed cells that pathogens cannot easily penetrate. When the skin is cut or broken, the risk of infection rises sharply, which is why wound hygiene matters.

Mucus lines the airways and digestive tract, trapping pathogens before they reach the internal tissues. Cilia — tiny hair-like projections on cells lining the airways — beat rhythmically to sweep mucus (and the trapped pathogens) up towards the throat, where it can be swallowed and destroyed by stomach acid. Smoking damages cilia, which is one reason smokers are more susceptible to respiratory infections.

Stomach acid (pH 1–2) kills most pathogens that enter via food or drink. Tears, saliva and mucus contain lysozyme, an enzyme that breaks down bacterial cell walls. These chemical barriers provide constant background protection without requiring the immune system to be activated.

Key Fact

First-line (non-specific) defences include skin (physical barrier), mucus and cilia (trap and sweep pathogens), stomach acid (kills pathogens in food), and lysozyme in tears/saliva (destroys bacterial cell walls). These prevent pathogens from reaching internal tissues.

The symptoms of infectious disease arise in two quite different ways depending on the type of pathogen. Bacteria primarily cause damage by releasing toxins — chemical waste products or deliberate biological weapons produced as the bacteria multiply. For example, the cholera toxin causes excessive water secretion from the gut wall; the toxins from Staphylococcus aureus can cause food poisoning. The bacteria themselves may not directly invade all tissues, but their toxins travel through the body and cause harm.

Viruses cause damage differently. Because they replicate inside host cells by taking over the cell’s ribosomes and other machinery, they destroy cells from within. When the new virus particles burst out (a process called lysis), the cell is killed. If large numbers of cells are destroyed, tissues stop functioning. The sore throat of a cold is partly caused by destroyed throat cells; the lung damage of severe influenza or COVID-19 is caused by destruction of lung epithelial cells by the virus.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions that ask you to ‘explain’ how a pathogen causes disease require causal language — use ‘because’, ‘so’ and ‘this means’ to link your points. A common mistake is to confuse bacteria and viruses: bacteria cause harm through toxins; viruses cause harm by destroying the cells they replicate in. Stating the correct mechanism for the correct type of pathogen is worth marks. For transmission questions, always name the specific route (e.g. airborne droplets, contaminated water) and do not just write ‘it spreads from person to person’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pathogens include bacteria (cause harm via toxins), viruses (destroy cells during replication), fungi (surface and systemic infections) and protists (e.g. Plasmodium via mosquito vectors). Communicable diseases can be transmitted; non-communicable diseases cannot.
  • Transmission routes include direct contact, airborne droplets, contaminated food/water and animal vectors. Each route suggests specific prevention strategies (vaccination, hygiene, vector control).
  • First-line non-specific defences — skin, mucus, cilia, stomach acid and lysozyme — prevent most pathogens from entering the body at all.

Vaccination provides specific, long-lasting immunity by priming the immune system with memory cells; far more effective than barriers once a pathogen has entered the body. Limitation: vaccination must be developed for each specific pathogen and requires population-level uptake for herd immunity to work. A balanced conclusion: barriers are essential frontline prevention; vaccination is the key tool for preventing specific diseases once barriers are insufficient.
Secure: Barrier defences explained and evaluated; vaccination mechanism and effectiveness evaluated; both limitations acknowledged.
Developing: Describes barriers and vaccines; some comparison made.
Emerging: Lists barriers; states vaccines work differently.

lessons.title: Immune System, Vaccination and Treating Disease
lessons.description: How the immune system fights infection, how vaccines work, antibiotic resistance and drug trials.
lessons.content_html:
The Body’s Internal Defence Force

When the body’s barrier defences are breached — a cut becomes infected, a virus is inhaled, a bacterium slips past stomach acid — a second, more sophisticated line of defence takes over: the immune system. Unlike the barriers that act against all pathogens indiscriminately, the immune response can identify specific invaders, mount a targeted attack, and — crucially — remember the encounter so future attacks are defeated faster. Understanding how this system works explains both why vaccines are so effective and why antibiotic resistance is so dangerous.

Antigens and the Specific Immune Response

Every pathogen carries proteins on its surface called antigens. These antigens are unique to that particular pathogen — different strains of influenza virus have different surface antigens, for example, which is why the flu vaccine needs updating regularly. When a pathogen enters the body, the immune system recognises the foreign antigens and mounts a specific immune response targeted at that particular pathogen.

Lymphocytes are the white blood cells responsible for the specific immune response. When a lymphocyte encounters the antigen that matches its receptors, it rapidly divides to produce a clone of identical cells. These cells then produce large quantities of antibodies — Y-shaped proteins precisely complementary to the specific antigen.

Key Fact

Antigens are foreign proteins on pathogens that trigger the immune response. Lymphocytes produce specific antibodies that are complementary in shape to those antigens. The antibody binds to the antigen, marking the pathogen for destruction.

How Antibodies Work

Antibodies destroy pathogens in three ways. First, they clump pathogens together (a process called agglutination), making it much easier for phagocytes to engulf and digest large numbers at once. Second, they neutralise toxins released by bacteria by binding to the toxin molecule and blocking its action. Third, they mark pathogens for destruction by other immune cells, a process called opsonisation — essentially tagging the pathogen so it cannot be missed.

Phagocytes complement the lymphocyte response by carrying out phagocytosis. Unlike lymphocytes, phagocytes are non-specific — they attack any foreign cell or particle. They are particularly effective at cleaning up pathogens that have been clumped or tagged by antibodies.

After an infection is overcome, most of the activated lymphocytes die off. However, some persist as memory cells. Memory cells may survive for years or decades in the bloodstream. They carry the ‘blueprint’ for producing the correct antibody for that pathogen.

If the same pathogen enters the body again, the memory cells recognise the antigen immediately and mount a response far faster and larger than the first time. The antibodies are produced so quickly that the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms develop — the person doesn’t even know they were reinfected. This accelerated secondary response is the biological basis for both natural immunity after infection and artificial immunity after vaccination.

How Vaccination Works

Vaccination exploits the immune system’s memory. A vaccine introduces antigens from a pathogen — typically via a dead or weakened version of the pathogen, a fragment of the pathogen, or a molecular instruction for producing the antigen — into the body. The immune system responds as if to a real infection: lymphocytes are activated, antibodies are produced, and memory cells are formed. The person has now acquired immunity without ever suffering the disease.

If enough people in a community are vaccinated, the pathogen cannot find susceptible hosts to infect and spread to. Even individuals who cannot be vaccinated (such as newborns or immunocompromised patients) are protected because the pathogen cannot circulate. This community-level protection is called herd immunity. The proportion of the population needed for herd immunity varies by how easily the disease spreads — measles requires very high coverage because it is extremely contagious.

Key Fact

Vaccines introduce antigens to trigger memory cell formation without causing disease. Herd immunity occurs when enough people are immune that a pathogen cannot spread easily, protecting vulnerable individuals who cannot be vaccinated.

Antibiotics — Effective Against Bacteria, Not Viruses

Antibiotics are medicines that interfere with the life processes of bacteria. They work by targeting bacterial structures that are absent in human cells — the bacterial cell wall is a common target. Because viruses do not have cell walls and reproduce entirely inside host cells using the host’s own cellular machinery, antibiotics have no effect on viruses. Prescribing antibiotics for a viral infection (such as the common cold or flu) does nothing to treat the patient and contributes to antibiotic resistance.

Antibiotic resistance develops through natural selection. Within a bacterial population, random mutations occasionally produce an individual that is less affected by an antibiotic. If antibiotics are used widely — especially if patients stop a course early or antibiotics are used in livestock farming — the susceptible bacteria are killed, but any resistant mutants survive and reproduce. Over generations, the resistant form becomes dominant in the population. The result is infections that cannot be treated by standard antibiotics — so-called ‘superbugs’ such as MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus).

Before a new medicine reaches patients, it must pass through a carefully staged testing process. The process begins with preclinical testing — new compounds are tested on cells and tissues in the laboratory (in vitro), then on animals to check for toxicity and initial effectiveness. Only if these early tests are promising does the drug progress to clinical trials involving human volunteers.

Clinical trials are conducted in phases. Phase 1 tests the drug’s safety on a small group of healthy volunteers — this establishes what dose range is tolerable and identifies any serious side effects. Phase 2 tests the drug on a larger group of patients with the target condition to assess whether it is effective and what the optimum dose is. Phase 3 involves much larger numbers of patients and uses a double-blind, placebo-controlled design: half the patients receive the real drug; half receive an inactive placebo. Neither patients nor researchers know who has received which, removing bias from the results.

The double-blind, placebo-controlled trial is the scientific gold standard for testing medicines because it controls for the placebo effect (where patients feel better simply because they believe they are being treated) and for researcher bias in recording outcomes. Only after passing all phases and receiving regulatory approval can a drug be licensed for widespread use. This rigorous process is an example of the scientific community using evidence and peer review to protect the public — a direct application of the ideas-about-science principle that hypotheses must be tested and results scrutinised before conclusions are accepted.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about the immune response, make sure you distinguish clearly between antigens (on the pathogen), antibodies (produced by lymphocytes), and memory cells (the long-term result). A very common error is to say that vaccines ‘give you the antibodies’ — they do not. Vaccines stimulate your immune system to make its own antibodies and memory cells. For drug trial questions, always explain why the placebo and double-blind design are necessary, not just what they are: they remove bias and control for the placebo effect.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Lymphocytes produce specific antibodies complementary to pathogen antigens. Memory cells formed after infection or vaccination allow a much faster secondary immune response, providing long-term immunity.
  • Vaccines exploit the immune memory by introducing antigens without causing disease. Herd immunity protects even unvaccinated individuals when enough of the population is immune.
  • Antibiotics kill bacteria by targeting structures absent in human cells; they have no effect on viruses. Antibiotic resistance arises through natural selection and is worsened by misuse. Drug trials use double-blind, placebo-controlled designs to produce unbiased evidence of effectiveness.

practice_questions.text: Explain why antibiotics are effective against bacterial infections but not against viral infections.

Over time, resistant forms become dominant in the population. Incomplete courses or overuse accelerates this process by selecting for resistant strains without eliminating them.

practice_questions.text: A new drug for treating a bacterial lung infection is being trialled. The trial uses a double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Suggest why this design is used and what it controls for.

Mastering: Double-blind means neither patients nor researchers know who receives the drug or the placebo; this removes researcher bias in recording improvements and removes the placebo effect (patients feeling better simply because they believe they are being treated). The placebo ensures any improvement in the drug group can be attributed to the drug itself rather than the psychological effect of receiving treatment. The design produces objective, unbiased evidence.

lessons.title: Lifestyle, Genes and Non-Communicable Disease
lessons.description: How lifestyle and genetic risk interact to cause cardiovascular disease, cancer and diabetes.
lessons.content_html:
Patterns in a Population

Epidemiologists — scientists who study the patterns of disease in populations — have assembled decades of data linking lifestyle behaviours to specific diseases. Countries where smoking rates are high tend to have higher rates of lung cancer. People with higher body mass index (BMI) have higher rates of type 2 diabetes. Communities with diets rich in saturated fat tend to have more cardiovascular disease. But here lies one of the most important thinking skills in science: just because two things are correlated does not mean one causes the other.

This lesson will build both your understanding of the science of non-communicable disease and your ability to interpret and evaluate risk-factor data critically — a skill that carries significant marks in your exam.

Risk Factors and Non-Communicable Disease

A risk factor is something that increases the probability of developing a disease. Risk factors can be lifestyle-related (smoking, diet, alcohol intake, physical activity), environmental (air pollution, UV radiation, carcinogens), or genetic (inheriting variants that increase susceptibility). Most non-communicable diseases result from multiple risk factors interacting, not a single cause.

Key Fact

Key lifestyle risk factors for non-communicable disease include smoking (cardiovascular disease, lung cancer), poor diet high in saturated fat and sugar (cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes), excessive alcohol consumption (liver disease, liver cancer), and physical inactivity (obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease).

Correlation vs Causation — A Worked Example

Consider a graph showing that in countries where more cigarettes are sold per person, the death rate from lung cancer is higher. This is a strong positive correlation. But does it prove smoking causes lung cancer? Not on its own — there could be confounding factors: perhaps countries with high smoking rates also have older populations, worse air quality, or poorer healthcare that detects cancer later.

Causation is only established when controlled experiments or very strong patterns across multiple independent studies rule out confounding factors. In the case of smoking and lung cancer, controlled studies, biological evidence (tobacco carcinogens directly mutate lung cell DNA), and consistent findings across decades and many populations together provide extremely strong evidence of causation. The scientific consensus is clear: smoking causes lung cancer. But the reasoning matters: correlation is the starting point, not the conclusion.

In exam questions you may be shown a table or graph of epidemiological data and asked to draw conclusions. When interpreting such data, follow these reasoning steps:

1. Describe the pattern: “As X increases, Y increases” — this is the correlation. 2. Note whether the correlation is strong or weak. 3. Consider whether a causal mechanism is plausible: could X biologically lead to Y? 4. Identify possible confounding factors that might explain the pattern without causation. 5. State whether the data alone is sufficient to conclude causation, and what additional evidence would strengthen the case.

For example: data shows that people who exercise less are more likely to have type 2 diabetes. Pattern: negative correlation between exercise and diabetes risk. Plausible mechanism: exercise improves insulin sensitivity and helps maintain healthy body weight. Possible confounding factor: people with poor diet (which also raises diabetes risk) may exercise less — both are linked to a third factor (overall lifestyle). Additional evidence needed: controlled studies where activity level is the only variable changed.

Cardiovascular Disease

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is one of the leading causes of death in the UK and worldwide. The underlying process in most CVD is atherosclerosis: fatty deposits, called plaques, accumulate inside the walls of arteries, narrowing the space through which blood can flow and making the artery walls stiff. The process is driven by high levels of cholesterol in the blood, particularly the LDL (“bad”) form, combined with damage to the artery lining caused by high blood pressure or smoking.

If a coronary artery (which supplies the heart muscle) becomes severely narrowed, the heart muscle receives insufficient oxygen during exertion, causing angina (chest pain). If a blood clot forms at a plaque and completely blocks the artery, the heart muscle is starved of oxygen and begins to die — this is a heart attack (myocardial infarction). If the blood supply to the brain is interrupted by a clot or a burst vessel, the result is a stroke.

Lifestyle changes — improving diet (reducing saturated fat and salt, increasing fruit and vegetables), taking regular aerobic exercise, stopping smoking, and reducing alcohol intake. These reduce blood cholesterol, blood pressure and body weight over time. Low risk with no side effects, but require sustained behavioural change.

Medical treatments — statins are drugs that reduce blood cholesterol levels by inhibiting the enzyme used to produce cholesterol in the liver. They significantly reduce the risk of heart attacks in people with existing CVD. Anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs reduce the risk of blood clots forming on plaques. Medication is effective but requires lifelong adherence and can have side effects.

Surgical treatments — stents are small mesh tubes inserted into a narrowed artery to hold it open and restore blood flow. Coronary artery bypass grafting uses a blood vessel taken from another part of the body to create a new route around a blocked artery. Surgical treatments are effective in severe cases but carry risks of infection, blood clotting and complications from general anaesthesia.

Cancer

Cancer occurs when the normal controls on cell division break down. Mutations in the genes that regulate the cell cycle cause cells to divide uncontrollably, forming a tumour. A benign tumour grows slowly in one location and does not invade surrounding tissue. A malignant tumour invades surrounding tissues and can break off and travel through the blood to establish new tumours elsewhere in the body — a process called metastasis.

Risk factors for cancer include: smoking (the carcinogens in tobacco smoke directly damage DNA in lung cells), UV radiation (causes DNA mutations in skin cells, increasing the risk of melanoma), certain viruses (human papillomavirus, HPV, is associated with cervical cancer), obesity, and inherited genetic variants that increase susceptibility. Not all cases of cancer have an identifiable risk factor — mutations can occur spontaneously during normal cell division.

Key Fact

Cancer is caused by mutations that lead to uncontrolled cell division. Benign tumours stay in one location; malignant tumours invade tissues and spread (metastasis). Risk factors include smoking, UV radiation, certain viruses and genetic predisposition.

Type 2 Diabetes, Obesity and BMI

In type 2 diabetes, body cells become less responsive to insulin — a condition called insulin resistance. As a result, blood glucose remains elevated after eating, damaging blood vessels and nerves over time. Obesity is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes because excess body fat — particularly around the abdomen — is associated with reduced insulin sensitivity. Diet high in refined sugars also raises blood glucose repeatedly, stressing the insulin-regulation system.

Body mass index (BMI) is used as an indicator of healthy weight. It is calculated as: $$\text{BMI} = \frac{\text{mass (kg)}}{\text{height (m)}^2}$$ A BMI above 30 is classified as obese. BMI is a population screening tool, not a perfect individual diagnostic — it does not distinguish between muscle and fat mass, for example. Nonetheless, population data consistently shows that higher average BMI correlates with higher rates of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Correlation-vs-causation questions are highly likely to appear in your exam because they carry marks for scientific reasoning, not just recall. When asked whether data shows causation, the default answer is: “correlation does not prove causation; additional controlled experiments are needed.” If asked to ‘suggest’ a reason for a trend in data, apply the biological mechanism you know (e.g. saturated fat raises cholesterol, which builds up in arteries). When evaluating CVD treatments, always include a benefit AND a risk for each approach — a one-sided answer will not reach the top mark band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Lifestyle risk factors (smoking, poor diet, alcohol, inactivity) are correlated with non-communicable diseases including CVD, cancer and type 2 diabetes. Correlation does not prove causation — controlled evidence and plausible biological mechanisms are needed to establish cause.
  • CVD results from atherosclerosis narrowing coronary arteries. Treatments range from lifestyle changes and statins to stents and bypass surgery, each with benefits and risks to evaluate.
  • Cancer is caused by mutations leading to uncontrolled cell division. Malignant tumours metastasise; benign tumours do not. Obesity and insulin resistance are key drivers of type 2 diabetes.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and Producers
lessons.description: How plants trap light energy to make glucose, and the resources producers need to grow.
lessons.content_html:
Producers and the Source of All Food

Walk into any greenhouse and you’ll find growers carefully controlling light levels, temperature and the air composition around their crops. They’re manipulating the same process that drives every food chain on Earth: photosynthesis. Organisms that carry out photosynthesis are called producers — they form the foundation of almost every food chain because they are the only organisms capable of capturing energy from sunlight and locking it into chemical bonds.

Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplast, an organelle containing the green pigment chlorophyll. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue wavelengths of light while reflecting green light — which is why leaves appear green. The reaction is endothermic: it takes in energy from the surroundings in the form of light.

Key Fact

Photosynthesis equation: $$\text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} \text{glucose} + \text{oxygen}$$
Symbol equation: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\). It is an endothermic reaction — it takes in light energy.

The Two Stages of Photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is a two-stage process. In the first stage, light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll and used to split water molecules, releasing oxygen as a by-product. In the second stage, the hydrogen released from water is combined with carbon dioxide to produce glucose. Both stages occur within the chloroplast.

The oxygen released in the first stage diffuses out of the leaf through tiny pores called stomata into the surrounding air. This oxygen is the source of almost all the oxygen in Earth’s atmosphere. The glucose produced in the second stage can be used immediately by the plant in respiration, or stored, or converted into other molecules.

Glucose made by photosynthesis has several important destinations within the plant. It may be broken down in respiration to transfer energy for life processes. Excess glucose is converted to insoluble starch for storage (starch does not affect osmosis because it is insoluble). Glucose is also converted to cellulose for building and strengthening cell walls.

When mineral ions such as nitrates are available from the soil, the plant can combine glucose-derived carbon skeletons with nitrogen to make amino acids, which are assembled into proteins. Glucose can also be converted into lipids (fats and oils) for energy storage in seeds. This explains why seeds are energy-rich foods: they store lipids made originally from photosynthetically produced glucose.

Limiting Factors and Rates of Photosynthesis

Three factors determine how fast photosynthesis can proceed: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature. Each can become a limiting factor — the one in shortest supply that prevents the rate from rising. On a graph of rate against one factor, the rate rises then plateaus: the plateau shows that a different factor has become limiting.

Light intensity — more light means more energy available for the light-dependent stage. As light intensity increases, the rate rises. At high intensity, it levels off because CO\(_2\) or temperature has become the new limiting factor. If a plant is moved further from a light source, the light reaching it decreases.

Carbon dioxide concentration — CO\(_2\) is a raw material for the carbon-fixing stage of photosynthesis. Increasing its concentration provides more molecules for the reaction, so the rate increases. In sealed glasshouses, growers can pump in extra CO\(_2\) from gas burners to raise yields.

Temperature — the reactions of photosynthesis are controlled by enzymes. Higher temperatures increase the kinetic energy of molecules, speeding up enzyme-substrate collisions. Above the enzyme’s optimum temperature (often around 25–30°C for many plants), the enzyme begins to denature and the rate falls sharply.

Key Fact

The three limiting factors interact. A graph plateau means a different factor is now limiting. To raise the rate further, you must increase whichever factor is currently limiting — not the one already in excess.

Resources That Producers Need: Minerals and Water

Producers need more than just light and CO\(_2\). They also require water, absorbed from the soil through root hair cells by osmosis, and mineral ions, absorbed by active transport. The most important mineral ions for plant growth are nitrates (to make amino acids and proteins) and phosphates (for DNA and cell membranes). A shortage of any of these resources limits growth regardless of how much light or CO\(_2\) is available.

Water absorbed by the roots travels upward through xylem vessels to the leaves. There it is used in photosynthesis or evaporates from cells and diffuses out through stomata — a process called transpiration. Transpiration keeps a continuous flow of water moving through the plant, carrying dissolved minerals to where they are needed.

Commercial growers use glasshouses to manipulate limiting factors and maximise crop yields year-round. Artificial lighting extends the ‘growing day’ and can be tailored to provide the red and blue wavelengths that chlorophyll absorbs most strongly. Gas burners add CO\(_2\) to the atmosphere inside the glasshouse. Heating systems maintain the optimum temperature for the crop being grown. Automatic irrigation delivers water directly to roots.

Each improvement has a cost, so farmers must weigh the extra income from increased yields against the running costs. If CO\(_2\) is already at an optimal level, spending money to increase it further will not raise the rate — light or temperature is then the limiting factor. Understanding which factor is currently limiting is therefore essential for making cost-effective decisions.

Key Fact

Producers need water (split in photosynthesis to release hydrogen and oxygen), CO\(_2\), light, and mineral ions including nitrates (for amino acids and proteins) and phosphates (for DNA). Transpiration drives water and mineral delivery through the xylem.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked to ‘explain’ the effect of a limiting factor, use a causal chain: state what the factor does to the rate, say why (link to the biochemistry — enzyme activity, raw material availability, energy supply), and then name what factor becomes limiting next. For 6-mark extended responses on limiting factors, compare at least two factors and explain why the graph plateaus. ‘Suggest’ questions will give you a novel context (e.g. a poorly ventilated greenhouse) — apply limiting factor logic rather than recalling a memorised answer.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Producers carry out photosynthesis in chloroplasts, converting CO\(_2\) and water into glucose and oxygen using light energy. The reaction is endothermic and the overall equation is \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\).
  • The rate of photosynthesis is controlled by three limiting factors: light intensity, CO\(_2\) concentration and temperature. Each can become the bottleneck, shown as a plateau on a rate graph.
  • Producers also need mineral ions (nitrates, phosphates) from the soil, absorbed by active transport, and water delivered through the xylem via the transpiration stream.

Disadvantages: high energy and installation costs, CO₂ use generates carbon emissions, and there is a diminishing return once one factor dominates. A well-run glasshouse makes informed decisions about which factor is currently limiting rather than increasing all factors regardless of cost.
