lessons.title: Ecosystems, Interdependence and Population Change
lessons.description: Food webs, biodiversity, abiotic and biotic factors and how populations respond to change.
lessons.content_html:
What Is an Ecosystem?

In the late 1980s, scientists tracking red fox populations across the Scottish Highlands noticed something unexpected: as foxes declined in certain areas, the populations of mountain hares — their prey — surged, only to crash again as overgrazing damaged the heather the hares depended on. One change rippled through an entire community. This is interdependence in action — a defining feature of every ecosystem.

Ecosystems are organised at four levels. Individual organisms of the same species living in the same area form a population. Multiple populations living and interacting together form a community. When that community interacts with the non-living environment, it constitutes the ecosystem.

Key Fact

Ecosystem levels: individual → population (one species) → community (many species) → ecosystem (community + abiotic environment). Every organism within a community is interdependent — change in one population affects others.

Biotic and Abiotic Factors

Abiotic factors are the non-living conditions that shape an ecosystem. Temperature, light intensity, moisture level, soil pH and wind speed are all abiotic factors. Biotic factors are the living influences: the presence of predators, availability of prey, disease, and competition with other species for resources.

A change in any one factor can cascade through the whole community. In rivers, ecologists monitor dissolved oxygen levels (abiotic) as a pollution indicator, and survey populations of pollution-sensitive invertebrates such as stonefly larvae (biotic indicator). A drop in dissolved oxygen triggers a fall in stonefly populations, which in turn affects the trout that feed on them. Tracking both types of factors together gives a richer picture of ecosystem health.

Key types of biotic relationship between organisms in a community include: predation (one organism kills and eats another), mutualism (both organisms benefit — for example, bees collect nectar from flowers while carrying pollen, benefiting both), and parasitism (one organism benefits while the other is harmed — for example, a flea living on a dog).

Organisms compete for resources whenever supply is limited. Animals compete for food, water, territory and mates. Plants compete for light, water, mineral ions and physical space. Competition can be intraspecific (within the same species — e.g. two male deer competing for a mate) or interspecific (between different species — e.g. red squirrels and grey squirrels competing for the same food sources in woodland). In the UK, the introduction of the larger, more competitive grey squirrel has contributed to the decline of the native red squirrel across much of England and Wales.

Food Webs and Energy Flow

Energy enters most ecosystems through sunlight, captured by producers (plants and algae) through photosynthesis. It then passes along a food chain through trophic levels: producer → primary consumer (herbivore) → secondary consumer (carnivore) → tertiary consumer (top predator).

At every trophic level, energy is lost to the surroundings through respiration, movement and heat. This is why less biomass is available at each successive level, and why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels. A single oak tree can support thousands of caterpillars, which support far fewer blue tits, which support very few sparrowhawks.

A food web shows all the interconnected food chains in a community. Because organisms typically eat several prey species and are eaten by several predators, changes in one population have complex knock-on effects. Removing a secondary consumer (a carnivore) typically causes its prey (primary consumer) population to increase rapidly, which then over-consumes the producer trophic level below. These cascading effects are sometimes called trophic cascades.

In the Yellowstone National Park in the USA, the reintroduction of wolves in the 1990s reduced elk populations and changed their grazing behaviour. This allowed riverside vegetation to recover, which stabilised riverbanks and even altered river channels — a striking example of how one species can reshape an entire ecosystem.

Key Fact

Energy is lost at every trophic level through respiration and heat, so biomass decreases up the food chain. Food webs are interconnected — removing or adding one species has knock-on effects throughout the whole community.

Predator–Prey Cycles and Population Change

Predator and prey populations are closely linked. When prey is plentiful, predators have more food, so their population rises. More predators mean more prey are eaten, so the prey population falls. With less food, predator numbers then decline, allowing the prey to recover — and the cycle repeats. These oscillating cycles, offset in time, are a classic pattern in ecology and can be modelled graphically with the predator curve always lagging slightly behind the prey curve.

Population size is also affected by density-dependent factors such as food supply, disease and competition, which intensify as populations grow. Populations are also affected by abiotic events like drought, fire or severe winters, which can cause sudden, large crashes in numbers regardless of population density.

Biodiversity and Why It Matters

Biodiversity refers to the variety of species within an ecosystem. High biodiversity confers resilience: if one species declines, others can often fill its ecological role, preventing the whole system from collapsing. A wheat monoculture has very low biodiversity; a native wildflower meadow has very high biodiversity and is far more resilient to pests, drought and disease.

Human activities including deforestation, habitat fragmentation, pollution and over-hunting have reduced biodiversity globally. Conservation strategies aim to reverse this: protected nature reserves maintain habitats, breeding programmes support endangered species, and rewilding projects introduce keystone species (such as beavers in parts of Scotland) that engineer new habitats and support many other species.

Key Fact

High biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable and resilient. Human activities reduce biodiversity; conservation programmes (reserves, breeding programmes, rewilding) aim to protect it. Biodiversity loss increases the risk of ecosystem collapse.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to ‘explain’ the effect of removing a species from a food web, trace the change through at least two trophic levels using causal language: ‘because’, ‘therefore’, ‘this means’. For ‘suggest’ questions involving novel ecosystems you haven’t studied, apply the same principles: identify the trophic level affected, predict the direction of change (increase or decrease), and explain the mechanism. In extended-response questions on biodiversity, examiners expect you to evaluate conservation methods — weigh benefits against difficulties, not just list strategies.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ecosystems are organised into individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems. Organisms are interdependent through predation, mutualism and parasitism, and compete for limited resources.
  • Biotic and abiotic factors both affect population size. Predator–prey cycles produce oscillating, offset population graphs. Food webs show how removing one species has knock-on effects throughout the community.
  • Biodiversity makes ecosystems more resilient. Human activities threaten biodiversity; conservation strategies including reserves, breeding programmes and rewilding aim to protect it.

practice_questions.text: Name one biotic factor and one abiotic factor that can affect the size of a population.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any correct biotic factor (e.g. predator availability, disease, food supply, competition) AND one mark for any correct abiotic factor (e.g. temperature, light intensity, moisture level, soil pH). Both required for the mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a predator–prey cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: When prey population rises, predators have more food so their numbers increase; increased predation reduces the prey population, so predator numbers then fall — producing oscillating cycles offset in time.
Secure: As prey increases, predators increase; then prey decreases causing predators to decrease.
Developing: When there is more prey there are more predators; when prey decreases so do predators.
Emerging: They go up and down together.

practice_questions.text: In a moorland food web: heather → mountain hare → red fox. Explain what would happen to the heather population if a disease killed most of the red foxes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Fewer foxes means the mountain hare population increases because hares are eaten less often. More hares consume more heather, so the heather population decreases. This is a trophic cascade — the loss of a predator causes overgrazing by its prey.
Secure: Hares increase because foxes eat fewer of them; more hares eat more heather so heather decreases.
Developing: Hare numbers go up; heather goes down because hares eat it.
Emerging: Heather decreases.

practice_questions.text: Compare the effects of a high-biodiversity ecosystem and a low-biodiversity monoculture in their ability to recover from a disease that wipes out one plant species.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: In a high-biodiversity ecosystem, other plant species can fill the ecological role of the affected species — herbivores have alternative food sources and the ecosystem structure is maintained. In a monoculture, all plants are the same species so the disease eliminates the entire food supply for primary consumers, causing collapse of the food web. High biodiversity provides resilience; low biodiversity increases vulnerability.
Secure: High biodiversity — other species survive and take over; monoculture — all plants affected, so collapse likely.
Developing: More species = more resilient. One species = disaster.
Emerging: More biodiversity is better.

practice_questions.text: A nature reserve in the UK wants to reintroduce a predator species that became locally extinct 100 years ago. Suggest two benefits and one potential problem of this rewilding programme.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Benefits: controlling prey population prevents overgrazing of vegetation; restoring the predator may increase overall biodiversity by creating a more complex food web. Problem: predator may prey on livestock outside the reserve, creating conflict with local farmers; or prey species may not have sufficient numbers to sustain the reintroduced population.
Secure: Two valid benefits with brief explanation; one valid problem.
Developing: One benefit and one problem, limited explanation.
Emerging: One benefit only.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the evidence that human activities are reducing global biodiversity, and assess the effectiveness of current conservation strategies in addressing this.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evidence includes well-documented habitat loss through deforestation reducing species richness; pollution and eutrophication killing freshwater species; over-hunting driving species to extinction. Conservation strategies such as protected reserves prevent further habitat loss; captive breeding programmes have prevented extinction of species like the Iberian lynx; rewilding (e.g. beavers returning to Scotland) restores habitats. However, reserves can become isolated islands; climate change threatens species even within protected areas; funding is insufficient globally. A balanced evaluation acknowledges both successes and ongoing challenges.
Secure: Names 2–3 human threats and 2–3 conservation strategies; evaluates at least one limitation.
Developing: Describes threats and strategies but evaluation is limited.
Emerging: Simple list of human threats; little evaluation.

glossary_terms.definition: A community of living organisms interacting with each other and their non-living environment in a particular area.
The way organisms in a community rely on each other for survival, including relationships such as predation, mutualism and parasitism.
All the organisms of one species living in a particular area at a particular time.
All the populations of different species living and interacting in the same area.
Non-living factors that affect the distribution and abundance of organisms in an ecosystem, such as temperature, light intensity, moisture, soil pH and wind speed.
Living factors that affect an ecosystem, such as availability of food, predators, disease and competition between organisms.
The position an organism occupies in a food chain: producer (level 1), primary consumer (level 2), secondary consumer (level 3), tertiary consumer (level 4).
Factors that limit population growth, including food supply, predation, disease and competition. As population density rises, their effect intensifies.
The variety of different species of organisms in an area, and the variety of habitats they occupy. High biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable.
